claims.text: The starting material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The starting HfNbTaTiZr is in the as-cast state.
Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C and strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has inadequate oxygen resistance for high-temperature exposure in air.
A thin, dense, alumina-forming surface coating can be deposited on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr by a method such as physical or chemical vapor deposition.
An anti-oxidation coating is an appropriate modification to consider for high-temperature use of this alloy system in air.
The coating will generate a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure.
The Al2O3 scale will act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion into the substrate.
Reduced oxygen ingress will prevent or suppress pesting of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The surface coating will not alter the alloy's bulk mechanical properties.
After 5 hours in air at 800 °C, coated specimens will exhibit significantly less oxidation or pesting than untreated specimens.
After coating and oxidation exposure, the alloy will retain its baseline room-temperature tensile ductility.
After coating and oxidation exposure, the alloy will retain its baseline yield strength near 1000 °C at strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
The claimed oxidation-protection boundary is air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours.
Long-term adhesion, thermal-cycling behavior, and coating-induced residual stresses remain undetermined.
A controlled comparison of coated and untreated specimens after identical air exposure can test the oxidation and mechanical-property predictions.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant oxidation reduction, or degradation of either specified mechanical property relative to the untreated control, would falsify the hypothesis.
